assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought cavity-QED strong coupling onto a chip, with dispersive readout and photon-mediated qubit coupling. It became the architecture behind essentially all superconducting quantum processors and the whole field of microwave quantum optics. The physics (a new, controllable regime of light-matter interaction) is the point, not the application, and the experiments are clean and reproduced widely.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf proposed it in 2004 and Wallraff et al. demonstrated strong coupling the same year; Schoelkopf's group built the transmon and dispersive-readout toolkit. Experimental leadership (Schoelkopf, Wallraff) plus the theory proposal (Blais) gives a fair three-person split, but Girvin's role is real and the omission is an unresolved allocation issue.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of independent confirmation across many laboratories; the interpretation is completely stable. Timing is delicate because the 2025 prize already honoured macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, so a second circuit prize so soon may look repetitive even though the science is distinct.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize and to the superconducting-circuit community; I have collaborations and programme ties in this area and would need to weigh conflict-of-interest rules.
Whether Girvin should be included over Blais, and the exact weight of the transmon versus the cQED architecture, is a matter of judgment I have not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for ion-trap quantum gates and its experimental realisation opened controlled many-body quantum engineering with trapped ions: gates, entanglement, digital and analogue quantum simulation. It showed that individual quantum systems can be controlled well enough to compute with.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller supplied the 1995 proposal; Blatt's Innsbruck group made the leading demonstrations of gates and entangled states, while Wineland (already a laureate in 2012) and others contributed experiments. A theory-plus-experiment pairing is natural; overlap with Wineland's earlier prize needs care in how the citation is worded.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with multiple groups and now commercial platforms showing high-fidelity gates. Recognition is timely and the science is stable.
uncertainties: Partial overlap with the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche) could make the committee view this as already recognised.
Experimental credit is distributed over several groups (Wineland, Monroe, Blatt, others), so the exact experimental laureate is debatable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Mott insulator transition and Hubbard-model physics in a clean, tunable system, and gave the community a general platform for strongly correlated many-body physics. It opened a new regime in which models can be built and probed with single-site resolution.
assessment.attribution: The Jaksch-Zoller-Cirac theory proposal and the Greiner-Bloch Mott insulator experiment are the key steps; Esslinger realised fermionic Hubbard physics. The credited list has five names, so a three-person cut necessarily omits strong contributors, especially Zoller and Cirac.
assessment.maturity: Mature and reproduced widely, with microscope-level imaging now standard. Open questions about reaching the low temperatures needed for d-wave physics do not undermine the discovery itself.
uncertainties: Choosing among five credited people is contested; the theory-versus-experiment split is not clean.
Whether the prize is for the platform or for specific discovered phenomena is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened the field of moire flat-band physics, with correlated insulators and superconductivity tuned electrically in a single device. It is a clear case of a prediction followed by a striking, reproduced experimental discovery that created a new research area.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands and the magic angle in 2011; Jarillo-Herrero's group discovered the correlated insulator and superconducting states in 2018. This is a natural theory-plus-experiment configuration, though Cory Dean and others contributed strongly in the moire materials field.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across groups, but the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated and the field is moving quickly, so a prize now is somewhat early.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism for the superconductivity remains unresolved.
Other experimental groups (for example Dean, Yacoby, Young) have contributions that are not within the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock with the magic-wavelength idea reached 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, enabling relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a path to redefining the second. It follows the earlier frequency-comb and ion-trap prizes but is a distinct and decisive advance in precision measurement.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic wavelength lattice scheme and demonstrated it first; Ye's group brought the clock to record accuracy and stability and developed the many-body clock physics. Both contributions are clear and the pair is a fair configuration. Other lattice-clock groups exist but are not in the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Very mature with multiple independent clocks agreeing, and the redefinition of the second is under discussion. Timely. I am outside my own expertise here and defer to colleagues in AMO and metrology.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as adequately distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
I have not independently verified the relative priority of the magic-wavelength proposal and the early experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical oscillators to the quantum regime through ground-state cooling, strong coupling, squeezing and entanglement of macroscopic motion. It connects directly to microwave and optical quantum control and to my own interests in coupling artificial atoms to phonons.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg, Aspelmeyer and Painter drove optical-domain control, while Cleland and Lehnert provided the circuit-based and piezoelectric quantum acoustics. Four credited names covers a broad field, so a three-person choice leaves out important experimental precedent.
assessment.maturity: Quantum ground-state and entanglement results are reproduced, but the field is still developing and applications in sensing are emerging. Somewhat early.
uncertainties: Which of the many parallel milestones (cooling, squeezing, entanglement) should define the prize.
Overlap with LIGO-era prizes and with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and its experimental observation, together with the quantum anomalous Hall effect in magnetic topological insulators, define topological materials with quantized edge transport. This is a clear physical idea with a robust experimental signature.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical prediction; Molenkamp realised the effect in HgTe wells; Xue observed the quantum anomalous Hall effect. The candidate bundles several distinct discoveries, and Bernevig, Zhang and Hasan are credited elsewhere in the longlist, so the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Mature and reproduced, with high-precision quantization in the anomalous Hall case. Recognition is timely, with the open question being which discoveries a single prize should include.
uncertainties: A compound discovery whose parts may need different recognition.
Credit disputes among theory proposals, especially for the HgTe prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) which is outside this entry's names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and the fault-tolerance theorems made large-scale quantum computation conceptually possible, and topological codes shaped modern hardware roadmaps. This is deep, original and lasting theory with experimental demonstrations now appearing in superconducting circuits.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane introduced the first quantum error-correcting codes and Kitaev the surface-code and topological idea; fault-tolerance thresholds involved others (Aharonov, Ben-Or, Knill, Laflamme, Gottesman). The three-person list is plausible but not the only fair one.
assessment.maturity: The theory is established, but I would be wary because complete experimental demonstration of fault-tolerant computation is still ahead. The discovery rather than the application is what matters, and this may be premature.
uncertainties: Whether below-threshold experiments are sufficient confirmation.
Allocation of credit among Shor, Steane, Kitaev, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme and others is disputed.
